article.headline: China's AI Trade Has Moved On From Consumer Internet to Chips
article.lede: KWEB, the $6.9 billion KraneShares ETF that defined China internet investing for a decade, is full of companies — Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu — that were the future once and are now mature platforms still nursing the scars of Beijing's 2021 regulatory crackdown. The companies actually building China's AI infrastructure — domestic chip designers, fab-equipment makers, and semiconductor material suppliers that China needs because it can no longer freely import Nvidia GPUs — list on a different exchange, track a different index, and are captured by a different ETF. That ETF is KSTR, and the performance gap between the two is impossible to ignore.
article.body:
**KWEB** — the KraneShares CSI China Internet ETF — was the canonical single-ticket for China internet exposure when Alibaba (BABA), Tencent (0700.HK), and Baidu (BIDU) felt like the future of the world's second-largest economy. That future arrived, then got badly complicated. Beijing's 2021 regulatory crackdown on its consumer internet sector — record antitrust fines, gaming restrictions, a cancelled Ant Group IPO, Didi forced off app stores days after its US listing — sent KWEB down roughly 58% from its February 2021 peak. By mid-2026 the five-year return stands at negative 49%. The fund holds roughly $6.9 billion in assets, which testifies more to inertia than conviction.

The “late 2010s-coded” label stings because it is accurate. KWEB's index — restricted by design to companies listed on Hong Kong, NASDAQ, or NYSE — captures China's consumer internet era: e-commerce, food delivery via Meituan (3690.HK), gaming, *super-apps*. These are platforms that monetize consumer attention and commerce. They are, in the language of the current moment, *AI users* — firms deploying large language models as product features, not companies building the hardware stack that makes AI possible.

KSTR — the KraneShares SSE STAR Market 50 Index ETF — tracks a different China entirely. The *SSE STAR Market* is Shanghai's answer to NASDAQ: a domestic listing venue for high-growth technology companies, launched in 2019, that cannot or will not list overseas. Its 50 largest constituents are overwhelmingly hardware. At roughly 14% of the fund, **Cambricon Technologies** (688256.SS) is the dominant position: the company designs *AI accelerator chips* for cloud training and edge inference, and its revenue grew more than 4,000% in the first half of 2025 as Chinese AI labs shifted from sanctioned Nvidia (NVDA) GPUs to domestic alternatives. Cambricon has confirmed day-zero software compatibility with DeepSeek's latest model. Hygon Information Technology (688041.SS), at roughly 11% of the fund, began as a joint venture with Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) to produce x86-compatible server CPUs; it has since expanded into GPU design and, after merging with state-owned HPC provider Sugon, now builds a full compute platform. Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment (688012.SS) — known as AMEC — makes the plasma etch and *CVD* tools that semiconductor fabs need, precisely the category targeted by US export controls on foreign suppliers.

The access problem is structural. KWEB's index methodology explicitly excludes *A-shares* — renminbi-denominated shares listed on mainland Chinese exchanges; it can only hold companies listed in Hong Kong or on US exchanges as *ADRs*. The most strategically consequential Chinese AI companies list domestically on the STAR Market because US IPOs became politically fraught after Didi's 2021 delisting disaster, and because domestic listing helps them retain state research contracts. KSTR, sub-advised by ICBC-UBS Asset Management, is the only US-listed ETF tracking the STAR 50 index. There is zero holdings overlap between the two funds. The sanctioned-equipment angle reinforces the distinction: AMEC's domestic etch tools fill the gap left by Applied Materials (AMAT) and Lam Research (LRCX) under US export controls, and that substitution trade lives entirely inside KSTR, not KWEB.

The performance gap has been stark. KSTR returned roughly 80% in the twelve months to May 2026; KWEB lost approximately 10% over the same period. The caveats are real: KSTR holds only about $116 million in assets against KWEB's $6.9 billion, making it prone to wider bid-ask spreads and steeper drawdowns, and its top two holdings account for roughly a quarter of the fund. Geopolitical risks also run in opposite directions — KSTR's chip companies sit on US export-control lists, constraining their access to leading-edge fabrication tools, while KWEB's ADR-listed holdings carry residual delisting risk under SEC audit-compliance rules. Neither is a safe harbour. But for an investor whose thesis is specifically that China's forced semiconductor self-sufficiency will generate extraordinary returns for the companies building that stack, KSTR is the precise instrument; KWEB is a category error.

concepts.definition: The Science and Technology Innovation Board (科创板), launched by the Shanghai Stock Exchange in July 2019 as China's domestic answer to NASDAQ. It allows high-growth technology companies — including those that are pre-profit or face barriers to overseas listing — to raise capital domestically. Its 50 largest constituents by market cap form the STAR 50 Index, which KSTR tracks.

A share of a company listed on the Shanghai or Shenzhen stock exchanges, denominated in Chinese renminbi and historically restricted to domestic investors. Foreign investors can access A-shares through specific programmes (QFII licences or the Hong Kong–Mainland Stock Connect), but many STAR Market companies are not covered by Connect, making US-listed ETFs like KSTR one of the few indirect routes for offshore investors.

American Depositary Receipt: a US-listed certificate, issued by a US bank, that represents ownership in shares of a foreign company. Chinese companies like Alibaba and Baidu trade as ADRs on NYSE and NASDAQ. ADRs carry an additional layer of geopolitical risk: the SEC's audit-inspection requirements have periodically threatened mass delistings of Chinese ADRs, most acutely during 2021–2022.

A specialised semiconductor designed to perform the matrix-multiplication operations at the heart of AI training and inference far more efficiently than a general-purpose CPU. Nvidia's H100 is the best-known example; Cambricon's Siyuan series is China's leading domestic equivalent, designed to train and run large language models without relying on sanctioned foreign silicon.

Chemical vapour deposition: a manufacturing process used in semiconductor fabrication to deposit ultra-thin films of material onto a silicon wafer. Along with plasma etching, CVD equipment is a critical step in building advanced chips, and it is among the categories covered by US and allied export controls targeting China's chip industry — making domestic suppliers like AMEC strategically important.

A mobile application that bundles a wide range of services — messaging, payments, ride-hailing, food delivery, social media — into a single platform. WeChat (Tencent) and Alipay (Ant Group) are the canonical examples. The super-app model dominated China's consumer internet era and remains the primary revenue engine for KWEB's largest holdings.

A shorthand for companies that deploy AI as a feature in existing products — e.g., Alibaba adding LLMs to its e-commerce search — as opposed to companies that manufacture the hardware or develop the foundational infrastructure that makes AI computation possible. The distinction matters for investors because in a supply-constrained environment, the hardware layer (chips, fab equipment) typically captures more pricing power than the application layer.

article.fact_check: Citrini's tweet describes KSTR as holding 'all the exciting Chinese AI companies,' which overstates the case. KSTR tracks the STAR 50 index — the 50 largest companies on Shanghai's innovation board — and its portfolio is dominated by semiconductor hardware: chip designers, fab-equipment makers, and memory-interface suppliers. Many of the most prominent Chinese AI companies by public profile (ByteDance, Moonshot AI, Zhipu AI, Manus AI) are either private or not STAR 50 constituents, and are therefore absent from KSTR. The fund is the best available US-listed vehicle for China's AI hardware buildout; it is not a comprehensive basket of Chinese AI.

ticker_baba.name: Alibaba Group Holding Limited
ticker_baba.blurb: Alibaba Group is a Chinese multinational technology company specializing in e-commerce, retail, cloud computing, and digital media. It operates major platforms like Taobao, Tmall, and Alibaba.com, and is a leader in China's online retail market. The company also has a significant presence in cloud services through Alibaba Cloud and in digital payments via Ant Group.
ticker_baba.recent: In the past 30 days, Alibaba's stock has seen upward movement driven by positive sentiment around its cloud business and cost-cutting measures. The company reported better-than-expected quarterly earnings, with revenue growth in its core commerce and cloud segments. Analysts have noted improved investor confidence amid regulatory easing in China.

ticker_0700-hk.name: Tencent Holdings Limited
ticker_0700-hk.blurb: Tencent Holdings Limited is an investment holding company that provides value-added services, marketing services, fintech, and business services in Mainland China and internationally. Its consumer business includes communications and social services (instant messaging and social networks), digital content (online games, videos, live streaming, news, music, and literature), fintech services (mobile payment, wealth management, consumer loans, and securities trading), and various tools. Tencent is one of the world's largest internet and technology companies by revenue and market capitalization, with a dominant position in China's social media and gaming markets.
ticker_0700-hk.recent: In the past 30 days, Tencent's stock price has shown volatility, trading in a range of approximately 460 to 480 HKD. The company is scheduled to report earnings on May 13, 2026, with analysts expecting continued revenue growth driven by its fintech and gaming segments. Recent news highlights include regulatory developments in China's tech sector and Tencent's ongoing investments in AI and cloud computing.

ticker_bidu.name: Baidu, Inc.
ticker_bidu.blurb: Baidu, Inc. is China's dominant internet search and AI technology company, operating a full-stack AI ecosystem that spans online search advertising, cloud infrastructure, and autonomous driving. Its core business generates the majority of revenue through search and marketing services, while its video-streaming subsidiary iQiyi contributes additional scale. Baidu has expanded aggressively into AI Cloud services and autonomous vehicle technology through its Apollo Go robotaxi platform, positioning itself as a leading AI infrastructure player in China with a market capitalization exceeding $53 billion.
ticker_bidu.recent: BIDU shares surged more than 20% in recent weeks following the announcement of a spin-off of its Kunlunxin AI chip unit and continued expansion of Apollo Go robotaxi services into Abu Dhabi and Dubai. Analysts have issued upgrades — including from Freedom Capital and BOC International — maintaining a Strong Buy consensus with average price targets around $165, citing robust growth in AI Cloud and non-marketing revenues even as core search advertising faces headwinds from macroeconomic pressures in China. The Kunlunxin spin-off has been the primary near-term catalyst, with investors increasingly pricing in long-term value from Baidu's autonomous driving and AI infrastructure ambitions.

ticker_3690-hk.name: Meituan (Class B)
ticker_3690-hk.blurb: Meituan is a Chinese technology-driven retail and local-services platform operating across mainland China, Hong Kong, Macao, Taiwan, and select international markets. Its Core Local Commerce segment encompasses food delivery, in-store dining, hotel and travel booking, while its New Initiatives segment spans bike and e-moped sharing, power-bank rental, micro-credit, and the Kuailv and Xiaoxiang Supermarket formats. The company also operates a B2B food distribution business and sells online marketing services to merchants on its platform. With roughly 111,000 employees and trailing twelve-month revenue of approximately CNY 406 billion (+8.1% YoY), Meituan is one of China's largest consumer-internet platforms by both scale and transaction volume.
ticker_3690-hk.recent: Meituan shares trade around HK$85.70 as of May 14, 2026, down roughly 38% from their 52-week high of HK$149.80, with analysts at Morningstar flagging intensifying competitive pressure that is expected to slow customer-acquisition growth (note published March 27, 2026). The company is scheduled to report earnings on May 26, 2026, which is acting as the near-term catalyst focus; the stock remains net-loss territory (trailing net income approximately −CNY 26 billion) and carries no dividend. Volume has been running well above the 35-million-share daily average, signaling heightened trader interest ahead of the print.

ticker_688256-ss.blurb: Cambricon Technologies Corporation Limited is a Chinese company specializing in the research, development, design, and sale of core AI chips for terminal devices. It offers cloud-based intelligent chips and boards, edge intelligence chips and boards, smart accelerator cards, and terminal intelligent processor IP. The company is a key player in China's semiconductor industry, focusing on artificial intelligence hardware.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_688041-ss.name: Hygon Information Technology Co., Ltd.
ticker_688041-ss.blurb: Hygon Information Technology Co., Ltd. is a Chinese semiconductor company founded in 2014 that designs high-performance processors, accelerators, and computing chip products for data centers, cloud computing, AI workloads, scientific computing, and industrial applications. The company offers a range of domestic x86-compatible processors targeting data center, mid-range enterprise, and workstation segments, positioning itself as a key domestic alternative amid China's push for semiconductor self-sufficiency. With roughly 3,333 employees and trailing revenue of ~16 billion CNY, Hygon has grown into one of China's most prominent chip designers with a market capitalization exceeding 800 billion CNY.
ticker_688041-ss.recent: As of May 14, 2026, shares closed at 325.20 CNY, down 6.60% on the day after trading as high as 358.80 over the prior 52 weeks, reflecting a 126% gain over the past year. The stock has pulled back from recent highs near 358.80 CNY, with elevated RSI of ~72 suggesting overbought conditions after a strong run. The next earnings date is slated for August 10, 2026; trailing twelve-month revenue grew ~60.6% year-over-year and net income rose ~26.9%, underscoring robust demand for domestic Chinese compute infrastructure.

ticker_amd.name: Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.
ticker_amd.blurb: AMD is a fabless semiconductor company that designs CPUs (EPYC for data centres, Ryzen for consumer PCs) and GPUs (Instinct for AI/HPC, Radeon for gaming and workstations). Under CEO Lisa Su, AMD has taken significant data-centre CPU market share from Intel with its EPYC server processors, which now command an estimated 30%+ of the x86 server CPU market. AMD's MI300X and MI350 AI accelerators compete directly with NVIDIA's H100/H200 family and are gaining traction with hyperscalers seeking GPU supply alternatives. All AMD chips are manufactured by TSMC.
ticker_amd.recent: AMD reported strong 2025 revenue growth led by EPYC and Instinct, with data-centre revenue crossing $12 billion annually. Forward P/E of ~32.6x on 63.8% projected EPS growth yields a PEG of 0.51 — compelling for a company with clear data-centre CPU momentum and an AI accelerator portfolio that is gaining customer adoption. NVIDIA's dominant CUDA ecosystem remains the primary competitive barrier for AMD's GPU ambitions.

ticker_688012-ss.name: Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment Inc. China (中微半导体设备(上海)股份有限公司)
ticker_688012-ss.exchange: Shanghai Stock Exchange (STAR Market / 科创板)
ticker_688012-ss.blurb: Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment Inc. China (AMEC) is one of China's leading domestic semiconductor equipment companies, specializing in plasma etch systems and metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) reactors used in integrated circuit and compound semiconductor manufacturing. Founded in 2004 by Gerald Yin, a former Applied Materials executive, AMEC was among the first Chinese firms to supply etching tools to leading-edge fabs. The company competes globally with Applied Materials, Lam Research, and Tokyo Electron, and has become strategically critical to China's push for semiconductor self-sufficiency under ongoing U.S. export control regimes.

ticker_amat.name: Applied Materials, Inc.
ticker_amat.blurb: Applied Materials is the world's largest semiconductor equipment company by revenue, supplying deposition, etch, ion implantation, and metrology tools used in chip fabrication at every major foundry and memory manufacturer. Unlike ASML (which focuses on lithography), Applied Materials covers the broadest range of wafer processing steps — most chips manufactured anywhere pass through multiple Applied Materials tools. The company also supplies solar and display manufacturing equipment. Its services business (AGS) provides recurring revenue through parts, upgrades, and maintenance contracts.
ticker_amat.recent: Applied Materials has benefited from sustained semiconductor equipment investment across logic (TSMC, Samsung, Intel), DRAM, and NAND capacity expansions. Forward P/E of ~27.3x on 27.1% projected EPS growth yields a PEG of 1.01 — right at the conventional fair-value boundary. Revenue for FY2025 exceeded $28 billion. U.S. export restrictions on advanced equipment to China have created some demand uncertainty but also pushed customers to accelerate domestic tool installations.

ticker_lrcx.name: Lam Research Corporation
ticker_lrcx.blurb: Lam Research is a leading semiconductor equipment company specialising in deposition (CVD, ALD) and etch systems — the tools that add and remove material layers during chip fabrication. Lam has particularly strong positioning in 3D NAND flash memory manufacturing, where its multi-layer deposition and etch tools are essential for building the hundreds of memory layers in modern NAND stacks. It also supplies critical tools for DRAM and advanced logic. Lam competes most directly with Applied Materials and Tokyo Electron, with each company holding dominant positions in different tool categories.
ticker_lrcx.recent: Lam Research trades at a forward P/E of ~36.2x on 30.7% projected EPS growth (PEG 1.18). The company has benefited from the NAND memory capacity buildout and is positioned to grow as 3D NAND layer counts increase — requiring more of Lam's deposition cycles per wafer. Revenue exceeded $17 billion in FY2025. Export restrictions to China have created some headwinds but domestic and non-China customer spending has partially offset the impact.

poster_citrini.blurb: Independent thematic-equity research firm founded in 2023 by James van Geelen, a self-taught investor who began his career in alternative healthcare before turning to public markets in 2018. Citrini publishes via paid Substack, runs a portfolio of long/short thematic baskets called the Citrindex, and has built a following on X for early calls on AI 'picks and shovels,' GLP-1 obesity drugs, and idiosyncratic trades such as a public short of Silicon Valley Bank in late 2022, months before its collapse. The firm now reports roughly ten employees and covers themes spanning AI, robotics, defence, healthcare and government policy.
poster_citrini.credibility_note: Track-record claims are largely self-reported through paywalled subscriber notes; the firm's '+131% since inception' and '+100% one-year' figures for its core portfolio cannot be audited externally. That said, several specific calls have been corroborated in the public press: the early 2023 AI hardware basket, the SVB short, and a February 2026 note on AI capex sustainability that was credited by Bloomberg with helping trigger an equity-market sell-off. Van Geelen, born around 1992, holds bachelor's degrees in biology and psychology from UCLA and is not a CFA charterholder; positions described in Citrini notes are the firm's own, and readers should assume the firm transacts in the names it covers.
